contracts.statement:
For $\tau\in\mathfrak H$, $z\in\mathbb C$ and $Q=e^{\pi i\tau}$,
$$\Theta(z\mid\tau):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}Q^{m^2}e^{2\pi imz}
=\prod_{n\ge1}(1-Q^{2n})(1+Q^{2n-1}e^{2\pi iz})(1+Q^{2n-1}e^{-2\pi iz}).$$
The series and product converge locally uniformly in each variable, uniformly on compact products. For fixed $\tau$, $\Theta$ is entire in $z$ with exactly the simple zeros $z=(1+\tau)/2+a+b\tau$, $a,b\in\mathbb Z$. In particular
$$\theta(\tau):=\Theta(0\mid\tau)=\prod_{n\ge1}(1-Q^{2n})(1+Q^{2n-1})^2\ne0.$$
Here $Q^2=q$; these cusp parameters must not be confused.
contracts.complete_local_proof_plan: For Im τ≥y₀>0, |Im z|≤M, the series is dominated by Σ_m exp(−πy₀m²+2πM|m|), a convergent Gaussian tail, so it is locally uniformly holomorphic in each variable. Call the displayed product Π. Its n-th grouped factor differs from1 by O(r^{2n−1}) on a compact product, where |Q|≤r<1 and e^{±2πiz} are bounded; normal convergence proves Π entire in z, holomorphic in τ and gives its zeros precisely from the factors. The first factor never vanishes. The second and third factors have zeros exactly at z=(1+τ)/2+a+bτ with respectively b≤−1 and b≥0. There is exactly one vanishing factor at each such point (Im τ>0 makes the lattice representation unique), and that factor has nonzero derivative, so all these zeros are simple. Termwise index shifts show Θ(z+1)=Θ(z) and Θ(z+τ)=Q^{-1}e^{-2πiz}Θ(z). The same laws for Π follow by cancelling its shifted product factors; the quotient for the second shift is (1+Q^{-1}e^{-2πiz})/(1+Qe^{2πiz})=Q^{-1}e^{-2πiz}, first away from the zeros and then everywhere by continuity. At z₀=(1+τ)/2, the m and −m−1 terms of Θ cancel, since their values are (−1)^mQ^{m²+m}; absolute convergence permits pairing. The two shift laws give Θ=0 at all Π zeros. Since each zero of Π is simple, local zero-order factorisation extends Θ/Π holomorphically through it, so this quotient is entire and doubly periodic in z. It is bounded on a compact parallelogram and hence throughout C; Liouville gives Θ(z|τ)=c(τ)Π(z|τ). No nonvanishing of Θ has been assumed. Set z=1/2 to get c(τ)=Σ_m(−1)^mQ^{m²}/∏_{n≥1}(1−Q^n)(1−Q^{2n−1}), whose denominator is zero-free. At z=1/4, odd m cancel in the series, giving Σ_m(−1)^mQ^{4m²}; the product is ∏_n(1−Q^{2n})(1+Q^{4n−2})=∏_n(1−Q^{4n})(1−Q^{8n−4}), by separating even and odd n in its first factor and using (1−u)(1+u)=1−u². Comparing with the z=1/2 formula at4τ gives c(τ)=c(4τ). Iteration and Q^{4^k}→0 show c(4^kτ)→1: in the ratio at z=1/2 the numerator tends to1 by the Gaussian tail estimate and the denominator to1 by the summable product estimates. Hence c(τ)=1. This proves the triple product, its exact simple zeros, and the zero-free theta constant at z=0. Finally, differentiating the two z-shift laws gives (Θ′/Θ)(z+1)=Θ′/Θ(z) and (Θ′/Θ)(z+τ)=Θ′/Θ(z)−2πi. Its derivative is doubly periodic and has a double pole at each proved simple zero, hence one double pole modulo the lattice; this is Stein–Shakarchi Corollary1.5, absorbed inline.

contracts.statement:
For $\tau\in\mathfrak H$ and $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}$,
$$\Delta(\tau)=q\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}(1-q^n)^{24},\qquad \Delta=(E_4^3-E_6^2)/1728.$$
The product converges locally uniformly for $|q|<1$; its factor after $q$ is holomorphic and zero-free in the unit disc and equals $1$ at $q=0$. Consequently $\Delta$ has integral Fourier coefficients and a simple zero at the cusp. Countable choice is assumed as in the Eisenstein special-value prerequisite.
contracts.complete_local_proof_plan: Define P(q)=∏_{n≥1}(1−q^n)^24 and F(τ)=qP(q). On |q|≤r<1, |(1−q^n)^24−1|≤(2^24−1)r^n; no factor vanishes, so the normal-product theorem proves holomorphy and nonvanishing of P throughout the disc, including P(0)=1. Finite-product logarithmic derivatives converge locally uniformly by the Weierstrass derivative theorem and the bound Σ nr^n/(1−r^n)<∞. Therefore (2πi)^{-1}F′/F=1−24Σ_{n≥1}nq^n/(1−q^n)=1−24Σ_{m≥1}σ₁(m)q^m=E₂(τ); the double regrouping is absolutely convergent and is justified componentwise by Fubini. For γ∈SL₂(Z), differentiate the nonzero holomorphic quotient R_γ(τ)=F(γτ)/[(cτ+d)^12F(τ)]. Its logarithmic derivative divided by 2πi is (cτ+d)^{-2}E₂(γτ)−12c/[2πi(cτ+d)]−E₂(τ)=0 by the E₂ law. Hence R_γ is a constant C_γ. Periodicity gives C_T=1; evaluation at τ=i gives C_S=1 because i^12=1 and F(i)≠0. Since S,T generate the modular group (and −I acts trivially in weight12), the transformation law holds for every γ by composition. Thus F∈S₁₂ with expansion q+O(q²). The dimension corollary gives dim S₁₂=1 and the existing discriminant lemma gives Δ∈S₁₂ with leading coefficient1, so F=Δ. For integrality, the coefficient of q^N in P equals that in ∏_{n≤N}(1−q^n)^24; later factors are1 modulo q^{N+1}. This finite coefficient is integral by the complex binomial theorem with integer coefficients. Its equality to the analytic Taylor coefficient follows by local uniform convergence of products and their derivatives at0. Therefore every coefficient of Δ=qP is integral.

contracts.statement:
With $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}$, the $j$-invariant has a Laurent expansion convergent for $0<|q|<1$,
$$j(\tau)=q^{-1}+744+196884q+21493760q^2+\sum_{n\ge3}c(n)q^n,\qquad c(n)\in\mathbb Z.$$
Equivalently $qj$ is holomorphic in the unit disc with integer Taylor coefficients and constant term $1$. Countable choice is inherited from the Eisenstein and discriminant proofs.
contracts.complete_local_proof_plan: Write Δ=qP(q), P(0)=1, using the product lemma. Since P is zero-free on the disc, qj=E₄(q)^3/P(q) is holomorphic there. The Eisenstein theorem gives E₄=1+240Σ_{n≥1}σ₃(n)q^n with integer coefficients, hence E₄³ has integer coefficients by the absolutely convergent complex Cauchy product. If P(q)=1+Σ_{n≥1}p_nq^n, all p_n are integers by the product lemma. Taylor expansion of P^{-1}=Σ b_nq^n and coefficient comparison in PP^{-1}=1 give b₀=1 and b_n=−Σ_{r=1}^n p_r b_{n−r}; induction proves b_n∈Z. Thus all coefficients of qj are integers and its Taylor series converges on |q|<1. To verify the displayed finite coefficients, multiply only the finite product factors required through degree3: P=1−24q+252q²−1472q³+O(q⁴), P^{-1}=1+24q+324q²+3200q³+O(q⁴). From σ₃(1)=1,σ₃(2)=9,σ₃(3)=28, E₄³=1+720q+179280q²+16954560q³+O(q⁴); multiplication gives qj=1+744q+196884q²+21493760q³+O(q⁴). This supplies a complete coefficient calculation rather than a table citation.

contracts.statement:
The weight-two Eisenstein series $E_2(\tau)=1-24\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_1(n)q^n$ satisfies $E_2(\tau+1)=E_2(\tau)$ and, for every $\gamma=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\in SL_2(\mathbb Z)$,
$$E_2\!\left(\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d}\right)=(c\tau+d)^2E_2(\tau)-\frac{6ic}{\pi}(c\tau+d).$$
In particular $E_2(-1/\tau)=\tau^2E_2(\tau)-\frac{6i}{\pi}\tau$, so $E_2$ is not a modular form of weight $2$.
contracts.complete_local_proof_plan: First derive ζ(2)=π²/6 without importing a choice assumption: the cotangent expansion is πcot(πz)=1/z+Σ_{n≥1}2z/(z²−n²). The normally convergent tail has linear coefficient −2Σ n^{-2}; division of the published sine and cosine power series gives πcot(πz)=1/z−(π²/3)z+O(z³), so comparison gives Σ n^{-2}=π²/6 ([[thm-mittag-leffler-expansion-of-pi-cotangent]], [[thm-complex-trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-power-series]]). Use the auxiliary half-normalisation H(z)=(π²/6)E₂(z), not the page's full lattice sum G_k. The k=2 Lipschitz identity and absolute q-series regrouping give H(z)=ζ(2)+Σ_{m≥1}Σ_{n∈Z}(mz+n)^{-2}. For ε>0 set H_ε(z)=½Σ′(mz+n)^{-2}|mz+n|^{-2ε}. On any compact subset of H there is C>0 with |mz+n|≥C max(|m|,|n|), by bounding |m| using the imaginary part and |n|≤|mz+n|+|m Re z|; the 8j points of the max-norm shell j give convergence by Σ j^{-1-2ε}. Absolute convergence permits reindexing, so H_ε(γz)=(cz+d)²|cz+d|^{2ε}H_ε(z). Put f_{m,ε}(t)=(mz+t)^{-2}|mz+t|^{-2ε} and I_ε(mz)=∫_R f_{m,ε}(t)dt. Pair (m,n) with (−m,−n), and subtract the row integrals to obtain H_ε(z)−Σ_{m≥1}I_ε(mz)=ζ(2+2ε)+Σ_{m≥1,n∈Z}[f_{m,ε}(n)−∫_n^{n+1}f_{m,ε}(t)dt]. This difference series is uniformly summable for ε∈[−1/4,1/4]: |∂_t f|≤(2+2|ε|)|mz+t|^{-3-2ε}, and |mz+t| is comparable uniformly on [n,n+1] to |mz+n| (both have imaginary part my≥y>0 and their difference has modulus≤1); a shell comparison reduces the majorant to Σ j^{-3/2}. Finite low shells are harmless. Applying the real FTC to real and imaginary parts supplies the row difference bound; the M-test permits ε→0 termwise. Since I_0(mz)=0 (primitive −1/(mz+t)), the difference tends to H(z). Translation and scaling give I_ε(x+iy)=y^{-1-2ε}I(ε), I(ε)=∫_R(t+i)^{-2}(1+t²)^{-ε}dt, and Σ_m I_ε(mz)=y^{-1-2ε}I(ε)Σ_m m^{-1-2ε}. Here I(0)=0 and I′(0)=−π: the difference quotients are dominated, for |ε|≤1/4, by (1+t²)^{-3/4}log(1+t²), whose tails are integrable; on each finite interval uniform convergence permits taking the derivative through the integral, and the tail bound extends it to R. A primitive of −log(1+t²)/(t+i)² is (1+log(1+t²))/(t+i)−arctan t, with endpoint difference −π. Finally integral comparison of the decreasing function t^{-1-2ε} gives Σ_m m^{-1-2ε}=1/(2ε)+O(1), without using analytic continuation of ζ. Thus Σ_m I_ε(mz)→−π/(2y), and H_ε(z)→H(z)−π/(2y). Take limits in the transformation identity and use Im(γz)=y/|cz+d|²: H(γz)=(cz+d)²H(z)−πic(cz+d). Multiplication by 6/π² proves the stated E₂ law; periodicity follows from its q-series. This local calculation supplies the formerly unproved regularisation limit; no citation is used in place of it.

contracts.statement: For even $k\ge4$ put $G_k(\tau)=\sum'_{(m,n)\in\mathbb Z^2}(m\tau+n)^{-k}$ and define the normalised Eisenstein series $E_k:=G_k/(2\zeta(k))$, where $\zeta(k)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-k}$ is the Riemann zeta function. Then $E_k$ is holomorphic on $\mathfrak H$ and $E_k(\tau)=1+O(q)$ as $\Im\tau\to\infty$. Separately, define the weight-two Eisenstein series by its $q$-expansion $E_2(\tau):=1-24\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_1(n)q^n$, $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}$; it defines a holomorphic function on $\mathfrak H$, is a quasimodular comparison object used in the discriminant product proof and in the counterexample item of the companion page.
contracts.complete_local_proof_plan: $G_k$ is holomorphic by the convergence lemma and $\zeta(k)$ is finite and positive for $k\ge4$ ([[thm-p-series-rational]]), so the normalisation is well defined; splitting off the $m=0$ term of the absolutely convergent sum and applying the Lipschitz formula ([[lem-lipschitz-formula-for-the-lattice-sum]]) to the terms with $m\ne0$ shows $E_k=1+O(q)$, the same computation that yields the Fourier expansion of [[thm-eisenstein-series-are-modular-forms]]. The series defining $E_2$ converges absolutely on $\mathfrak H$ because $\sigma_1(n)\le n^2$ and $\sum n^2|q|^n$ converges for $|q|<1$ by the ratio test, so $E_2$ is holomorphic.

contracts.statement:
The modular lambda function induces a biholomorphism
$$\bar\lambda:Y(2)=\mathfrak H/\Gamma(2)\longrightarrow\mathbb C\setminus\{0,1\}.$$
Let $Q^\circ=\{\tau\in\mathfrak H:|\Re\tau|<1,\ |\tau-1/2|>1/2,\ |\tau+1/2|>1/2\}$ be the interior of the standard ideal quadrilateral with vertices $\infty,-1,0,1$. Its restriction is a biholomorphism
$$\lambda:Q^\circ\longrightarrow\mathbb C\setminus((-\infty,0]\cup[1,\infty)).$$
Moreover $\lambda:\mathfrak H\to\mathbb C\setminus\{0,1\}$ is a regular covering whose deck group is $\bar\Gamma(2)=\Gamma(2)/\{\pm I\}$ acting freely and simply transitively on every fibre.
contracts.complete_local_proof_plan: First prove λ holomorphic in τ from its defining ℘ half-period series: on compact subsets of H the lattice estimate |mτ+n|≥C_K max(|m|,|n|) controls the normally convergent ℘ series, and half-period arguments stay uniformly away from lattice points; pairing terms gives summable O(max(|m|,|n|)^{-3}) tails. Each term is holomorphic in τ, hence so are e_j and their quotient, whose denominator never vanishes. Conjugating the same series and relabelling m↦−m gives λ(−bar τ)=overline{λ(τ)} (the half-period labels are preserved modulo lattice and sign). Γ(2)-invariance and the local quotient charts descend λ to a holomorphic map on Y(2). The fibre lemma makes it injective. For surjectivity define R(x)=256(1−x+x²)^3/[x²(1−x)²]. For any z≠0,1 choose τ∈H with j(τ)=R(z), since the finite values are attained off the cusp. The Legendre-j lemma gives R(λ(τ))=R(z). The six substitutions of the transformation lemma exhaust every fibre of R, including the exceptional ones: for a generic x all six orbit points are distinct and the cleared degree-six polynomial R(u)=R(x) is the product of their linear factors up to its nonzero leading coefficient; this factorisation continues to every x≠0,1 by equality of rational coefficient functions, and accounts for multiplicities when orbit points coincide. Thus some modular transform of τ maps to z. A bijective holomorphic map of Riemann surfaces is biholomorphic by the injective-derivative theorem. The torsion-free Γ(2) action and local charts give a regular quotient covering; λ is its composition with this biholomorphism. A deck transformation sends any chosen τ into its Γ(2) orbit, so agrees there with a Γ(2) transformation, and uniqueness from one point makes them equal globally. Finally establish the quadrilateral interface. Use Γ(2) reduction directly. For fixed τ, the set {|cτ+d|: γ∈Γ(2)} attains a positive minimum: restrict to denominators≤1, use the finite-lattice-pair lemma, and note that identity contributes1. Thus the Γ(2) orbit has a point of maximal height. Translate by T² to |Re τ|≤1. The two Γ(2) matrices with bottom rows (2,1) and (2,−1) would increase height if |2τ+1|<1 or |2τ−1|<1, so the representative belongs to closure Q. For uniqueness, a Γ(2) matrix has c even, d odd. If c≠0, its isometric disc |cτ+d|<1 has centre −d/c and radius1/|c|. A centre in (−1,0) or (0,1) is at distance≥1/|c| from both interval endpoints (d and c−|d| are nonzero integers), so that entire disc lies in the boundary disc with diameter [−1,0] or [0,1]. Centres cannot equal−1,0,1, since d is odd and c even; if a centre is outside [−1,1], its distance to the strip is≥1/|c|. Therefore |cτ+d|≥1 on closure Q and strictly>1 on Q°. If two closure-Q points are equivalent with one interior and c≠0, applying the height formula to the map and its inverse contradicts the strict inequality in one direction. If c=0, the map is translation by an even integer, which cannot identify distinct interior points or an interior point with a boundary point. This proves every orbit meets closure Q, interiors have no identifications, and no boundary orbit meets Q°. Its vertical boundary edges are T^{±1}(iy), and the semicircle edges are L_±(iy), L_±=(1 0;±1 1), y>0. The transformation formulas and 0<λ(iy)<1 give negative values on the verticals and values 1/λ(iy)>1 on the semicircles. Hence every w in the slit plane, being attained in H, has a closure-Q representative that lies in Q°, so the restriction is onto the slit plane. It is injective by the fibre and fundamental-domain assertions. If τ∈Q° has real λ, reflection −bar τ is also in Q° and has the same value. Uniqueness forces τ=−bar τ, whence τ=iy and λ(τ)∈(0,1). Thus no interior point maps to either deleted real ray. Local inverse holomorphy follows from injectivity. In particular λ(1+i)=−1 lies on the vertical boundary, explaining why the former claim that Q° maps onto the twice-punctured plane was false.
